lede: Charge flows round a circuit whenever it is switched on, and the current tells you how fast. This topic puts a number on how much charge has flowed, in coulombs, and shows what happens to the voltage when cells are joined end to end, including one put in the wrong way round.
can: Calculate charge, current or time with Q = I × t
Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting
Work out the voltage of cells in series, allowing for a reversed cell

text: Charge, current and cells in series

md: Switch on a torch and charge flows round its circuit. The current says how fast. Know how fast and for how long, and you know how much charge has passed. Join cells end to end and their voltages add, but only if they face the same way.

md:
**Charge** is measured in **coulombs (C)**. **Current** is the charge passing a point each second, measured in **amperes (A)**: 1 A means 1 coulomb every second.
So the charge that passes is the current multiplied by the time:
**charge = current × time**, or $Q = I \times t$

prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point in the circuit, in coulombs?
explain: Q = I × t = 2 × 5 = 10 C. Every second 2 coulombs pass, and there are 5 seconds.

title: Why the time must be in seconds
md: Because the ampere is defined per second: one ampere is one coulomb every second. Put a time in minutes into $Q = I \times t$ and the answer comes out 60 times too small.

title: What examiners saw
md: **Summer 2025 Foundation:** in an electrical calculation, a significant minority did not convert 10 minutes into seconds and lost marks for it. The same slip was reported in Summer 2024.

prompt: A heater is switched on for 2.5 minutes. How many seconds is that?
explain: 2.5 × 60 = 150 s. Half a minute is 30 seconds, so the decimal is no problem once you multiply.

md:
**Question.** A phone charges with a current of 1.5 A for 20 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows. [4]
**Step 1: the equation.** Q = I × t
**Step 2: time in seconds.** t = 20 × 60 = 1200 s
**Step 3: substitute.** Q = 1.5 × 1200 = 1800
**Step 4: the unit.** Q = 1800 C

prompt: Your turn, same four steps. A torch bulb takes a current of 0.6 A for 5 minutes. How much charge flows, in coulombs?
explain: t = 5 × 60 = 300 s, then Q = 0.6 × 300 = 180 C. The conversion line is the one that earns the second mark.

md:
The same equation rearranges two ways:
**current = charge ÷ time**, $I = Q \div t$
**time = charge ÷ current**, $t = Q \div I$
The counter above shows 600 C in 4 minutes. Convert first: 4 × 60 = 240 s. Then I = 600 ÷ 240 = 2.5 A.

prompt: A charge of 90 C passes through a heater in 45 s. What is the current, in amperes?
explain: I = Q ÷ t = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 A. The time was already in seconds.

title: Watching it for CCEA
md: The video is made for other exam boards. If it says potential difference, that is what CCEA calls voltage. If it shows an equation linking energy, charge and voltage, that equation is not on the CCEA Double Award specification. Cells joined the wrong way round are CCEA's own, so no video covers them: they are section 6.

prompt: A lamp in a circuit lights up. What happens to the charge that flows through the lamp?
options: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
it is used up by the lamp
it is stored inside the lamp
answer: it carries on round the circuit and back to the cell
explain: Charge is not used up. The lamp takes energy from the charge, and the same coulombs flow on round the circuit. That is why the current is the same all the way round a single loop.

md:
A **battery** is two or more cells joined **in series**, end to end. When they all face the same way, the positive plate of one next to the negative plate of the next, their voltages **add**.
A cell turned the wrong way round pushes against the others, so its voltage is **subtracted**. Two 1.5 V cells facing opposite ways give 1.5 − 1.5 = **0 V**, and a lamp joined to them stays off.

prompt: Four 1.5 V cells are joined in series, and one of them is the wrong way round. What is the total voltage, in volts?
explain: Three cells add and the reversed one subtracts: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5 = 3 V. The reversed cell cancels one of the others.

task: Join two batteries end to end with a light bulb to make a loop, and put a voltmeter across the two batteries. Read the voltmeter. Now select one battery and reverse it. Watch the voltmeter and the bulb. The simulation has no charge counter, so it cannot check Q = I × t; use it for the cells.

prompt: Two 9 V batteries are joined in series and one is turned round. What does a voltmeter across both of them read, in volts?
explain: 9 − 9 = 0 V. The two push equally in opposite directions, so the bulb goes out.

md:
Calculate charge with Q = I × t, and rearrange it to find a current or a time.
Put any time in minutes or hours into seconds before you substitute.
Say what 1 A means: one coulomb passing a point every second.
Add the voltages of cells in series, subtracting any cell that faces the wrong way.

Charge usually comes as one part of a longer electricity question, worth [4]: the equation, the substitution, the answer and the unit C. The first mark is for writing Q = I × t before any number; if the time is in minutes, converting it is part of the working. Cells in series come with a diagram: check which way each cell faces before adding. Stuck? Write the equation and put the time into seconds.
